newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - NZ First heads for centre.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - NZ First heads for centre.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Nov 26 - David Lange, a couple of days after the general election last month said: "We've ended up in the absurd position of being putty in the hands of Winston (Peters), who marches his party to the left on some issues, to the right on others, but never along the centre because that would be pedestrian".
But now, a month into coalition talks, NZ First is searching for the centre line.

That's evident from its modification of its compulsory superannuation scheme, re-labelled a "second tier superannuation scheme". It has ditched the government guarantee, which was originally to be offered on investment returns. And NZ First, recognising that the scheme would have penalised young people saving for a home, is proposing that contributors be allowed to borrow against the fund at low or zero interest rates to buy their own homes, secure vocational training or set up businesses.
Clearly, NZ First has found both National and Labour unsympathetic to its original scheme.
Rather than abandon it, the party has decided to float off a modified version.
Tucked away in the fine print is an apparent retreat from its goal of substituting the scheme for the second round of tax cuts in July 1997.

That suggests NZ First recognises it cannot bulldoze the priority item in its election manifesto on to the agenda of a coalition government. It may still have the freedom to propose legislation in Parliament on the issue -- and see whoever stands up to salute.

It probably could count on ACT (which has itself called for the implementation of a compulsory superannuation scheme), and possibly some other individual MPs. But the proposal could get a thorough going-over in the select committee, out of which some sort of consensus might emerge -- and that, after all, is what MMP is supposed to be about.

Rather than condemning the coalition negotiations for taking too long, as most New Zealanders are doing, they should welcome the process if it is bringing the NZ First negotiators face-to-face with some of the cold reality of government.
Despite the Lange view, New Zealanders may not have reduced themselves to putty in Winston's hands.
Both Labour and National, by saying "no" independently of each other to the more fanciful of Peters' election pledges, are forcing NZ First back towards the centre.
That has significant implications for those who became concerned that in any coalition arrangement, the tail could wag the whole creature.
The reality is that a party commanding only 13 percent of the total vote -- even though it holds the balance of power -- cannot expect to ram through measures that are unacceptable to the majority.
NZ First, as a coalition partner, may be able to exercise a veto on policy issues. This, too, could be limited, not just in circumstance, but in scope.

In cabinet, for example, it may hold up to five seats, but the majority will be held by the larger coalition partner, and that means under the rules of Cabinet collective responsibility a decision taken by the majority is binding on the minority.
The minority can as a last resort walk out; but the electorate could wreak vengeance if the walk-out provoked a snap election without much justification.
Peters started out on the coalition negotiations hoping to extract a binding agreement from his prospective coalition partners on the programme for the next three years.

Both National and Labour negotiators have been awake to the risks. They are aware that if they compromise on what are the fundamental principles of their own parties, they not only have given hostages to NZ First's fortunes, but put themselves in peril of crucifixion at the hands of their own supporters.
So the lesson in future coalition negotiations for those parties seeking to join a larger political party is: don't flaunt untradeable bottom lines.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
